Outside
out'-sīd
n. and adj. (the exterior surface or part; the outer edge of a camp, a wall, a cup)
From out and side. The Authorized Version uses it in two settings that interpret each other: the outside of Midian's camp, where Gideon stood in the dark, and the outside of the Pharisee's cup, which he washed while the inside stayed foul.

Biblical Definition

Our Lord fixed the meaning of this word for the church: “Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye make clean the outside of the cup and of the platter, but within they are full of extortion and excess” (Mat 23:25). The charge is not that they cleaned the outside — the outside of a cup ought to be clean — but that they cleaned only the outside and were content. The remedy He gives is not less washing but a different order: “cleanse first that which is within the cup and platter, that the outside of them may be clean also” (Mat 23:26). Inside-out is the gospel's direction, and it is the reason regeneration precedes reformation in Reformed theology; a new heart produces a clean life, and no amount of scrubbing produces a new heart. Luke records the same words at a Pharisee's table, where our Lord had declined the ceremonial washing before meat (Luk 11:39). The Old Testament uses of outside are literal and set the scene: Gideon “came unto the outside of the camp in the beginning of the middle watch” (Jdg 7:19) with a trumpet, a pitcher and a lamp, and God routed a host with three hundred men who never drew a sword; and Ezekiel's measuring man begins with “a wall on the outside of the house round about” (Eze 40:5), because the holy is bounded, and the first thing a temple has is an edge.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines outside as the external part of a thing; the part, end or side which forms the surface; and figuratively, the superficial appearance.

expand to see more

OUTSIDE, n. The external part of a thing; the part, end or side which forms the surface.

1. Superficial appearance; as a fair outside.

2. The utmost; the furthest limit; as, that is the outside of the sum.

SUPERFICIAL, a. Being on the surface; not penetrating the substance of a thing; shallow; contrived to cover something.

Key Scripture

Mat 23:25 — "Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye make clean the outside of the cup and of the platter, but within they are full of extortion and excess."

Mat 23:26 — "Thou blind Pharisee, cleanse first that which is within the cup and platter, that the outside of them may be clean also."

Luk 11:39 — "And the Lord said unto him, Now do ye Pharisees make clean the outside of the cup and the platter; but your inward part is full of ravening and wickedness."

Jdg 7:19 — "So Gideon, and the hundred men that were with him, came unto the outside of the camp in the beginning of the middle watch; and they had but newly set the watch: and they blew the trumpets, and brake the pitchers that were in their hands."

Modern Corruption

The cup is still washed on the outside; only the criteria of a clean outside have changed.

expand to see more

It is easy for a conservative church to read Matthew 23 as a rebuke of somebody else — the ritualist, the legalist, the man with the wrong externals. But the outside of the cup is whatever the surrounding company inspects, and every generation inspects something. Where the marks of belonging are correct opinions, correct alarm at the correct enemies, correct vocabulary, and a presentable family, a man may keep the whole of that outside spotless while extortion and excess sit inside untouched. Our Lord's word is addressed to the most doctrinally careful party of His day, and it lands nearest to those most confident it is not about them.

The order our Lord commands is the whole of the answer, and it is the order of the Reformed ordo salutis: cleanse first that which is within. Regeneration, then repentance and faith, then a life increasingly conformed — the outside genuinely made clean, but made clean second and from within. Any programme that reverses this produces what Matthew 23 describes: whited sepulchres, beautiful outward, and within full of dead men's bones.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew qatseh (H7097), the end, edge or outside; Greek exothen (G1855), from without, the outside; esothen (G2081), from within.

expand to see more

Hebrew qatseh (H7097) — end, extremity, outside edge; Judges 7:11, 7:17, 7:19, the outside of the armed camp.

Hebrew chuts (H2351) — the outside, the street, that which is without; Ezekiel 40:5.

Greek exothen (G1855) — from outside, the exterior; Matthew 23:25-27, Luke 11:39.

Greek esothen (G2081) — from within, the inward part; the word set against it in the same sentences.

Greek harpage (G724) — extortion, ravening, plunder; what filled the inside of the clean cup.

Usage

"“Ye make clean the outside of the cup” — and were content with it."

"“Cleanse first that which is within” — the order is the doctrine."

"“Unto the outside of the camp” — three hundred men, and not a sword drawn."
